question: A farmer presents 14 hours after sustaining a deep, contaminated laceration from a rusty implement. He has never received tetanus toxoid. What is the most appropriate management?

answers.text: Primary closure after wound irrigation and tetanus toxoid injection only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primary closure is contraindicated in contaminated wounds >6–8 hours old — infection risk is too high. Additionally, a never-vaccinated patient needs both tetanus toxoid AND tetanus immunoglobulin.

answers.text: Wound irrigation, debridement, delayed primary closure after 3–5 days, tetanus toxoid plus tetanus immunoglobulin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Contaminated wounds older than 6–8 hours should be cleaned and debrided but left open for delayed primary closure. A patient with no prior tetanus vaccination needs both active (toxoid) and passive (immunoglobulin) prophylaxis.

answers.text: Immediate closure under general anaesthesia with prophylactic antibiotics; no tetanus cover needed as the wound will be cleaned

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Immediate closure of a contaminated 14-hour wound will seal in bacteria and risk serious infection. Tetanus prophylaxis is determined by vaccination history, not wound cleanliness alone.

answers.text: No closure; apply antiseptic dressing and give oral antibiotics only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antiseptic dressings and antibiotics alone without debridement and a wound management plan are insufficient. Tetanus prophylaxis is also mandatory here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key rules: contaminated wounds older than 6–8 hours are not primarily closed. A patient never vaccinated against tetanus needs toxoid (active) PLUS immunoglobulin (passive) prophylaxis.
Well done. Contaminated wounds > 6–8 hours old need debridement + delayed primary closure. Unvaccinated patients require both tetanus toxoid and immunoglobulin.
